description: Every planet has secrets, and we’re here to crack the case. Team Sherlock Biosphere investigates the evidence hidden in Earth’s systems, from rising temperatures to changing oceans. We spot the patterns, follow the leads, and connect the dots to solve the mystery of how our planet is changing.
summary:
TerraTrend is an interactive web app that turns decades of NASA satellite measurements into trend investigations anyone can follow. Users spin a 3D globe and open a “case file” for any of eight Earth system variables: sea level, Greenland ice loss, CO₂, warming, wildfire, groundwater, Arctic sea ice and ocean heat.

Each case file answers the challenge’s four questions. What is changing: the variable and its source mission, such as GRACE-FO, Jason-3, OCO-2, MODIS or GISTEMP. Where: every trend is pinned to its measurement location, with 42 clickable regional zones telling local stories. How much: Sen’s slope gives the yearly rate in real units. Is it significant: a Mann-Kendall test we coded from scratch reports S, Z and the p-value, flagging a trend only when p < 0.05. Terra, a built-in AI assistant, explains any trend or method in plain language.

These changes affect food security, coastal cities and freshwater for billions of people, yet the evidence sits in archives most people never open. TerraTrend gives students, educators, journalists and policymakers a rigorous yet approachable way to see what the data actually says.
details:
What it does and how it works
TerraTrend lets anyone investigate how Earth is changing. You spin a 3D globe and click a hotspot to open a case file on one of eight variables: sea level, Greenland ice loss, CO₂, surface warming, wildfire, groundwater, Arctic sea ice and ocean heat. Each case file gives you the key finding, why it matters, an interactive trend chart and the full statistics behind it.

Every investigation follows four steps:

  1. Select a variable on the globe.
  2. Fetch the data. Saved NASA and NOAA records open the panel instantly while live data from NOAA GML and Open-Meteo ERA5 loads in the background.
  3. Test the trend. A Mann-Kendall test decides whether it is significant (p < 0.05) and Sen’s slope measures the yearly rate in real units such as mm, ppm, Gt or ZJ.
  4. Pin the trend to where it was measured. Clicking anywhere on the globe also brings up one of 42 regional stories, from Lake Chad to the Himalayan glacial lakes.

Terra, a built-in AI assistant powered by Claude, answers questions about any variable, region or method. It can also add buttons to its replies that fly the globe straight to the right panel.

Benefits
TerraTrend answers all four challenge questions in one view: what is changing, where, by how much and whether it is significant. It shows the full test results next to a plain-language reading, so a student and a scientist can trust the same screen. A progress tracker invites you to explore all eight variables.

Intended impact
Rising seas, shrinking aquifers and warming oceans affect food, water and safety for billions of people. The evidence is real, but most people will never open a NASA archive or read a research paper. TerraTrend puts that evidence in front of students, teachers, journalists and policymakers so they can check what the data says for themselves.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step. Three.js r160 drives the 3D globe and a Canvas 2D globe takes over when WebGL isn’t available.
  • Statistics: We wrote the Mann-Kendall test and Sen’s slope from scratch, with no external library.
  • Data: NASA GRACE-FO, Jason-3 / Sentinel-6, OCO-2 / OCO-3, GISS GISTEMP v4, Terra / Aqua MODIS, ICESat-2, AIRS and NSIDC records, plus NOAA NCEI and Argo float data. Live feeds come from NOAA GML and Open-Meteo ERA5.
  • AI: Claude Haiku through the Anthropic API, called from a Vercel serverless function so the API key stays off the browser.
  • Hosting: Vercel. No special hardware was needed.

Creativity
We turned trend analysis into detective work. Each variable is a case with a finding, evidence and a verdict on significance. The globe shows where each change is happening instead of leaving it as a line on a chart. Terra makes the site feel like a conversation that can take you anywhere on the planet.

Factors we considered

  • Rigour: Climate data is noisy and rarely normally distributed. We chose Mann-Kendall over linear regression because it is rank-based and robust to outliers, and it is the standard test in Earth science.
  • Reliability: Every variable keeps saved real data to fall back on and every live request has a time limit. We host Three.js ourselves so a blocked CDN can’t break the globe.
  • Accessibility: The app works fully on mobile with touch controls and still runs on devices without WebGL.
  • Honesty: Every dataset names its source. Terra is told never to make up numbers and to say when it isn’t sure.
  • Openness: With no build step and almost no dependencies, anyone can run, check or extend the project.
